title: Sobriety and Conceptual Shifts
description: Caravaggio, “Bacchus,” 1596, via Wikimedia Commons. What Does it Mean to be “Sober”? Language shifts. Sometimes the change leaves a gaping void in our ability to understand the world and our place in it. Consider, for instance, the virtue term ‘sober.’ When you hear that word, what do you envision? You might say someone is sober when you mean that he isn’t currently drunk. Or maybe you thought that someone is sober in the sense of having ‘sobered up,’ having formed a stable disposition not to partake at all in the relevant intoxicant. Sometimes such people live in a “sober house.” Or, third, you might think of someone as sober when he is solemn, mature, not prone to frivolity. Gimli the dwarf of the Lord of the Rings books—but not the movies, where he is played for comic effect—is sober. The first usage— ‘sober’ as not currently drunk—names a present state, not a stable trait. Habitual drunkards can be sober in that first sense. Of the latter two, it is only the middle that deals with intoxicants, and so only the middle that stands a chance to be the virtue of sobriety. But importantly, that second use of the term—having a stable disposition not to partake in the relevant intoxicant at all —does not express the traditional virtue of sobriety. Sobriety in the Traditional Sense To be sober , in the traditional sense, is to be a person stably disposed to partake of intoxicants in the right measure, for the right reasons, in the right occasions.

title: On Grit and Fortitude
description: Sant, “Courage, Anxiety, and Despair: Watching the Battle,” 1850, via Wikimedia Commons. An Introduction to Grit and Fortitude Stories valorizing perseverance through difficulty and trial—sometimes called grit—have existed as long as we have records, as far back as Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey . Grit continues to be celebrated in our culture in stories of those who have endured great hardship. Is grit alone enough? Should we seek something more? Grit emerged onto the scene in psychology roughly two decades ago. Popularized especially by the work of Angela Duckworth, founder of the Character Lab . Grit, understood as perseverance in long-term goal pursuit, relates to both energy and endurance. Those with grit tend to be more successful in school and career, and they tend to have better health outcomes. Interest in grit was especially high in the United States military in order to improve resilience among officers . These psychologists seem to believe that grit is good. Others agree and have taken to calling it a performance virtue. Given this modern virtue’s two main facets, energy and endurance, grit seems to align closely with Thomas Aquinas’ views on fortitude. Aquinas considers fortitude to have two main facets as well, endurance and ‘attack’, understood as preparing for and engaging with difficult tasks . So far then, it seems that grit and fortitude are similar, with attack relating closely to maintaining energy. However, given Aquinas’ views of virtue, fortitude is subject to reason and ideally to right reason. Grit has no such constraint. Does this matter? If so, why? title: Boasting: The Big I and the Little You
description: By Fr. Basil Cole, O.P., and Fr. John Baptist Ku, O.P. Woodville, “Politics in an Oyster House,” 1848, via Wikimedia Commons. What is boasting, according to St. Thomas Aquinas? In a job interview, you must sell yourself. While it would be counterproductive to overstate your abilities in an incredible way, you must promote yourself vigorously. In social situations, by contrast, such self-promotion could be disastrous. And yet, it can be sensible to recommend ourselves to others in a subtle manner. Discerning how to behave in such situations requires prudence. So, how much can we boast? Isn’t boasting a sin? If so, how grave a sin is it? In this article, we will turn to St. Thomas for guidance on these questions. In the question on boasting in the Summa Theologiae , St. Thomas offers this definition of boasting: Jactantia (boasting) seems properly to denote the uplifting of self by words: since if a man wishes to throw (jactare) a thing far away, he lifts it up high. And to uplift oneself, properly speaking, is to talk of oneself above oneself. This happens in two ways. For sometimes a man speaks of himself, not above what he is in himself, but above that which he is esteemed by men to be; and this the Apostle declines to do when he says (2 Corinthians 12:6): ‘I forbear lest any man should think of me above that which he sees in me, or anything he hears of me’ ( ST II-II, q. 112, a. 1 ). Thus, Paul spoke well of himself on occasion, yet he spoke honestly. But “in another way a man uplifts himself in words, by speaking of himself above that which he is in reality.” Here then, there is a certain dishonesty in exaggerating one’s merits.
